To summarize, the key findings of our research, stated in one sentence that includes all relevant information, are that

1) there is evidence that FeNO measurements are influenced by several factors that need to be taken into account when interpreting FeNO values; 2) FeNO is increased at the early stage of the disease in infants with family atopy/atopic disease, in those with recurrent wheezes and in infants with cystic fibrosis; and 3) FeNO values measured during the first 2 y of life could predict future respiratory morbidity in infancy and early childhood.
FeNO can be measured in the first 6 months of life with the tidal breathing technique and that FeNO values are increased in children with recurrent wheezes.

FeNO is a non invasive and safe tool for measuring bronchial eosinophilia in infants, that it can be measured both with the single breath technique and with the tidal breathing technique, that FeNO is influenced by several methodological factors and by the exposure to pre and postnatal risk factor for asthma, and that FeNO measurements can be useful to assess the presence of bronchial inflammation also in infants with other respiratory diseases.
In summary, our research is concerned with
the study of the role of eosinophilic inflammation in the development of asthma in the early life.
the development of a reliable method to measure Fe NO in young infants and with the evaluation of its clinical and epidemiological application.
the measurement of exhaled nitric-oxide (NO) in children and the relationship of this measurement with the development of asthma and other respiratory diseases.
